Incorporating the Beige Book alongside the FOMC, FSR, and SLOOS tilts the assessment more negative. District reports for March–April indicate broad-based declines in economic activity, with consumer spending notably weaker at auto dealers and general retailers, and tourism-related employment heavily hit. Manufacturing remained under pressure amid uncertainty, while price pressures were generally muted, with input costs influenced by freight, metals, tariffs, wages, and natural gas; crop price moves varied by commodity. Although some districts still cited shortages of skilled labor in certain niches (supportive of pockets of wage pressure), these were overshadowed by widespread job losses.

This Beige Book read corroborates SLOOS evidence of sharply tighter bank credit across C&I (all firm sizes), CRE/multifamily, and select consumer categories, reinforcing a restrictive credit backdrop just as the FOMC highlights impaired credit flows and “considerable risks.” The FSR’s improvement in market functioning tempers tail risks, but district-level weakness and tighter intermediation point to a weaker near-term outlook for activity and employment with subdued inflation.

Netting these, the sentiment shifts more negative than before.
